keywords: do i qualify for a grant
title: SASSA grants: which ones exist and who qualifies
owner_summary: If someone in your house is 60 or older, is caring for a child under 18, or cannot work because of a disability, SASSA may owe them a monthly grant and most people who qualify never ask. From April 2026 the old age grant is reported as R2,400 a month (R2,420 from age 75) and the child support grant as R580 per child, but those figures come from news reports, so confirm them at the SASSA office or on sassa.gov.za before you count on them. Every grant has a means test: SASSA looks at your income and, for the older person's grant, what you own. Applying is free and nobody may charge you to help.
applies_when: someone in your household is over 60, has a child under 18, has a disability, or you are not sure what you qualify for
not_when: you are already receiving every grant you qualify for, or your only question is the R370 SRD grant (see the SRD entry)
steps: List everyone in your house with their age and whether they work, are disabled, or care for a child: each one may qualify for a different grant

Match them to the grant: older person's grant from age 60; child support grant for the main carer of a child under 18; disability grant for an adult who cannot work for more than 6 months; foster child and care dependency grants for children in care or with severe disabilities

Check the means test before you go: SASSA counts your income (and assets for the older person's grant), and the limits are published on sassa.gov.za and change each year, so do not rely on a number from a website

Take your 13-digit South African ID, the child's birth certificate for a child grant, proof of income if you have any, and 3 months of bank statements if you have an account, to your nearest SASSA office
Apply in person and keep the receipt SASSA gives you; it is your proof of the date you applied, and a grant is paid from that date if approved
Never pay anyone to apply for you: applying is free, and SASSA's toll-free line 0800 60 10 11 can tell you where the nearest office is
cost: free to apply; grant amounts reported for April 2026 are R2,400 (older person, 60 to 74), R2,420 (75 and over) and R580 per child (child support), from news reports of the 2026 Budget, so confirm on sassa.gov.za (checked 2026-10-30)

keywords: deduction i did not agree to
title: What may be taken off a SASSA grant, and how to stop the rest
owner_summary: Only one deduction may come off a social grant: a funeral policy premium from an insurer registered under the Long-term Insurance Act, no more than 10% of the grant, and only if you gave consent. Nothing may be deducted from a child support, foster child or care dependency grant at all. SASSA itself says any other deduction, including airtime, loans or a second funeral policy, is unlawful. If your grant arrives short, you can dispute it by SMS to 34548 with your ID number and the name of the company, or at a SASSA office, and SASSA has made insurers refund people who never agreed.
applies_when: your grant arrives with less than the full amount, or a company says it has permission to deduct from it
not_when: the money is leaving a bank account you chose to pay a debit order from; that is a debit order you can stop at the bank, not a grant deduction
steps: Check your grant payment against the full amount: if it is short, write down the amount missing and the month it started
Find the name of the company taking it: it shows on the SASSA statement at the office or on your bank statement if the grant is paid into a bank account
Ask yourself the three tests SASSA uses: is it a funeral policy from a registered insurer, is it 10% of the grant or less, and did you sign or agree to it; if any answer is no, it is unlawful
Dispute it by SMS to 34548 with your ID number and the company's name, or report it at your nearest SASSA office with your receipt and statement
Phone the company and cancel the policy in the same week, and ask for the cancellation in writing by SMS or email
If the money is not refunded, lodge a complaint with the National Financial Ombud on 0860 800 900, which is free; never pay a 'consultant' to get your money back
cost: free to dispute; the only lawful deduction is one funeral premium of at most 10% of the grant, with your consent (SASSA statements 2025 to 2026, checked 2026-10-30)

title: Claiming UIF after losing work
owner_summary: If you were employed and your employer deducted UIF, you can claim unemployment benefits after being retrenched, dismissed or your contract ending, but not if you resigned. You must claim within 12 months of your last day, so do not wait. You earn roughly 1 day of benefit for every 4 days you worked, up to 365 days, paid at between 38% and 60% of your salary depending on how much you earned, lower earners get the higher percentage. Claim online on the Department of Employment and Labour's uFiling site or at a labour centre; it is free and you need the UI-19 form from your employer.
applies_when: you were employed, UIF was deducted from your pay, and you lost the job in the last 12 months
not_when: you resigned, you were never registered for UIF, or your last day was more than 12 months ago
steps: Ask your old employer for a completed UI-19 form and a salary schedule the week you leave; by law they must give it to you, and the claim cannot start without it
Register as a work seeker with the Department of Employment and Labour, which is part of the claim
Claim online at ufiling.labour.gov.za (register with your ID and the details on your UI-19) or take your ID, UI-19, payslips and bank details to the nearest labour centre
Claim within 12 months of your last working day; the fund turns away late claims
Expect roughly 1 day of benefit per 4 days worked, at 38% to 60% of your pay (lower earners get the higher rate), paid in instalments while you keep signing the continuation forms
If the employer never paid over your UIF, claim anyway and tell the labour centre: the fund can pursue the employer, and you can call the UIF line on 0800 030 007 to check progress
cost: free to claim; benefit is 38% to 60% of your salary, 1 day per 4 days worked up to 365 days, claim within 12 months (Department of Employment and Labour via calculator and guide sites, checked 2026-10-30)

title: The indigent register: free basic electricity and water
owner_summary: Every municipality keeps an indigent register: a list of low-income households that get free basic services, usually 50 kWh of electricity a month (some give up to 60 kWh), a free water allowance and relief on rates. The income limit is set by each municipality and differs a lot (Ekurhuleni published about R10,479 a month in 2026, smaller towns far less), so ask yours. Once registered, a prepaid household claims the free token each month, with Eskom customers dialling *130*269#. It costs nothing to apply, and the free units do not carry over, so claim them every month.
applies_when: household income is low, someone in the house gets a grant or pension, and you pay for electricity or water
not_when: your household income is clearly above your municipality's limit, or you live in a place where someone else holds the municipal account and will not help you register
steps: Go to your municipality's customer care office and ask for the indigent register or 'free basic services' application; the income limit and the form are theirs, not Eskom's

Take your ID, proof of income (a grant slip or affidavit that you have no income), your latest municipal statement or a prepaid electricity token, and 3 months of bank statements if you have an account; most municipalities ask for these
If the property is not in your name, ask the owner for a letter or affidavit saying you live there; municipalities usually accept it
Ask when the free electricity starts and how to claim the token: Eskom customers dial *130*269# on the first of each month, municipal customers get the token where they buy electricity
Claim the free units every month; unused units do not carry over
Diary the renewal: most registers must be renewed every year, and approval can take a few months, so apply before you fall behind
cost: free to apply; typically 50 kWh of electricity a month (up to 60 kWh in some municipalities) and a free water allowance; the income limit is set by each municipality, for example about R10,479 a month in Ekurhuleni in 2026 (checked 2026-10-30)

title: The R370 SRD grant: apply, check status, appeal
owner_summary: The Social Relief of Distress grant is R370 a month and has been extended to 31 March 2027. It is for adults with no other grant and almost no income; the threshold used in checks is reported as R624 a month, but a court case has challenged the rules, so confirm it on srd.sassa.gov.za. You apply only online, with your ID number and a cellphone number in your name, and you check the status on the same site every month. If you are declined, appeal on the site within the window it shows. Applying is free; anyone asking for a fee is a scam.
applies_when: you are 18 to 59, get no other grant or UIF, and have little or no income
not_when: you receive another SASSA grant, UIF, or a regular income above the threshold shown on srd.sassa.gov.za
steps: Go to srd.sassa.gov.za on your phone and choose 'Apply'; it asks for your ID number and a cellphone number registered in your name
Give banking details for an account in your own name if you can; it speeds up payment, and you can change them only on the site, never by WhatsApp
Check your status on srd.sassa.gov.za each month under 'Check status' with your ID and cellphone number; SASSA re-checks income every month, so a month can be declined even after approval
If declined, read the reason on the status page and appeal on the site within the time it shows; attach proof if the reason is wrong
Keep your cellphone number active and in your name; SASSA uses it for OTPs and messages
Never pay anyone to apply or 'unlock' your grant, and never share your ID number or banking details on a WhatsApp group; the toll-free SASSA line is 0800 60 10 11
cost: free to apply; the grant is R370 a month, extended to 31 March 2027 (2026 Budget); the R624 income threshold is from third-party reports, confirm on srd.sassa.gov.za (checked 2026-10-30)

title: Severance pay when you are retrenched
owner_summary: If you are retrenched (dismissed because the business is shrinking or closing), the Basic Conditions of Employment Act section 41 says you must get at least one week's pay for every completed year of service, on top of notice pay and any leave you are owed. The employer must also give you a UI-19 for UIF. If the money is not paid, you can refer the dispute to the CCMA for free on 0861 16 16 16; you do not need a lawyer. Severance is yours before anything else is settled, so never sign a final document until the amounts are written on it.
applies_when: you have been retrenched or told the business is closing, and you have worked there at least one full year
not_when: you resigned or were dismissed for misconduct; severance does not apply, though UIF may
steps: Count your completed years with the employer and multiply by one week's pay: that is the legal minimum under section 41 of the BCEA, and a better package agreed in consultation replaces it
Ask in writing for a breakdown before your last day: severance, notice pay, leave pay, and the UI-19 for your UIF claim
Check the breakdown against your payslips and do not sign a settlement that says 'full and final' until every amount is correct
If the severance is not paid, phone the CCMA on 0861 16 16 16 and ask to refer a dispute on form LRA 7.11; it is free and the CCMA's case officers help you fill it in
Keep every letter, SMS and payslip in one place; the CCMA will ask for them
Claim UIF at the same time: a retrenchment is the clearest case for unemployment benefits, and the two do not cancel each other out
cost: free to claim and free to refer to the CCMA; the legal minimum is one week's pay per completed year of service (BCEA section 41, checked 2026-10-30)

title: Do you need to file with SARS, and is a refund waiting
owner_summary: If you earn under the tax threshold you pay no income tax, and if your employer deducted PAYE anyway, or you paid medical aid or retirement contributions, a refund may be sitting at SARS. The threshold for the year to 28 February 2026 was R95,750 for people under 65; third-party tax sites report R99,000 for the year that started 1 March 2026, so confirm on sars.gov.za. Filing season for the 2026 year ran from July to 23 October 2026, with auto-assessments issued in early July: if SARS auto-assessed you and it is right, you do nothing and the refund is paid; if it is wrong, you file the return on eFiling or the SARS MobiApp.
applies_when: you earned a salary with PAYE deducted, paid medical aid or retirement fund contributions, or got an auto-assessment SMS
not_when: your only income is a social grant or cash piece jobs under the threshold and no tax was ever deducted; there is nothing to refund
steps: Check your IRP5 from your employer for the 'PAYE' line: if tax was deducted and your yearly income is near or under R95,750 (year to 28 February 2026), a refund is likely
Register on sars.gov.za for eFiling or download the SARS MobiApp with your ID and tax number; if you have no tax number, the registration creates one

If SARS sent an auto-assessment, open it in the app and check the income and deductions against your IRP5 and medical aid certificate; if correct, you do nothing and any refund is paid into the bank account SARS has for you
If it is wrong or you were not auto-assessed, file the ITR12 return in the app before the filing deadline SARS publishes each year (23 October 2026 for the 2026 season)
Make sure the bank account on your SARS profile is in your own name; refunds are only paid to a verified account
Never pay a 'tax refund agent' who messages you on WhatsApp; SARS does not use agents like that, and its contact centre is 0800 00 7277
cost: free to file; the tax threshold was R95,750 for under-65s for the year to 28 February 2026 and is reported as R99,000 for the 2026/27 year by third-party sites, confirm on sars.gov.za (checked 2026-10-30)

title: Know what comes in and on which day
owner_summary: You cannot plan a month you cannot see. Write down every rand that comes in and the day it lands: salary, grants (SASSA publishes the payment dates each month, older persons first, then disability, then children's grants), piece jobs, money from family. For income that changes, use the lowest month of the last 3 as your planning number, never the best one. The day money lands is the day every plan in this app starts: bills, the money put aside and the family amount all move on that day, before the month can eat it.
applies_when: you are not sure what you earn in a month, your income changes, or money comes from more than one place
not_when: you get one fixed salary on one fixed day and already know the amount after deductions
steps: Write one line per source of money: who pays, how much, and the day it lands (SASSA's grant dates for the month are on sassa.gov.za and in the news on the first days of each month)
For piece jobs or hustle money, look at the last 3 months and write the lowest month; that is the number you plan on
Add them up: that is your month, after deductions, not before
Circle the biggest landing day; that becomes your payday for every rule in your plan
Keep this page next to your month plan and fix it whenever a source changes
Never plan on money that is promised but not yet in your hand; a loan or a 'maybe' job is not income
cost: free

title: Write down a week of spending, every rand
owner_summary: Nobody knows where their money goes until they write it down for 7 days: every taxi, every R12 airtime, every loaf. The point is not to judge, it is to see. One line per spend in your phone's notes app or a notebook: what and how much. At the end of the week add it up and circle the 3 biggest lines. Those 3 are where your month plan starts. Most people find one line they did not know was that big, usually airtime bought in small pieces, transport, or bank fees.
applies_when: you run out before the month ends and cannot say exactly where the money went
not_when: you already keep a full record and the month plan fits; go straight to the month plan
steps: Open the notes app on your phone (or take a small notebook) and make a page called 'Week 1'
Each time money leaves your hands, write one line the same day: 'taxi R18', 'airtime R12', 'bread R19'
Include the small things and the cash ones: airtime, data, electricity, a cooldrink, money given to a child
On day 7, add it all up and write the total at the bottom
Circle the 3 biggest lines; those are the lines your month plan has to deal with first
Before you change anything, do a second week: one week can be unusual, two weeks is a pattern
cost: free

title: The three pots: bills, aside, the rest
owner_summary: A budget that works on a prepaid phone has three pots, decided on payday before anything is spent. Pot 1 is the bills and debts that must be paid, each with its date. Pot 2 is the money put aside: the cushion, and the family amount if there is one. Pot 3 is everything else: food, transport, airtime, electricity. Take pot 1 and pot 2 off the top on the day money lands; pot 3 is what is left, divided by the weeks until the next payday. If pot 1 alone is more than the money, do not invent savings; that is a debt problem, and the owed list comes first.
applies_when: money lands once or twice a month and runs out before the next payday
not_when: the bills already exceed the income; then the owed list and the hardship steps come before any budget
steps: Write what lands on payday at the top of a page, after deductions, using the lowest month if income changes
List pot 1 under it: rent, electricity, school, every debt minimum, each with the day it is due, and add them up
Write pot 2: the amount going to the cushion (GoalSave or a separate pocket) and the fixed family amount, moved on payday itself
Subtract pots 1 and 2 from the top number: what is left is pot 3, and divide it by the number of weeks to the next payday for a weekly food-and-transport number
Pay pot 1 and move pot 2 on the day money lands, then live on the weekly number
After 2 weeks, compare the plan with your spend log and fix the lines that did not fit; never fix a gap by borrowing
cost: free

title: Find every fee on last month's statement
owner_summary: Bank fees are a bill nobody reads. Get last month's statement in your banking app and add up every line that is a fee: monthly fee, ATM withdrawals, declined or 'unpaid' debit orders, SMS notifications, cash deposits. A declined debit order is the one that hurts: the bank charges you for the failure and the company tries again. GoTyme's published fee page lists R0 monthly, R3 for a declined debit order and cash out at a till, so confirm your own bank's numbers in its app. The free versions of most things are: withdraw cash at a supermarket till, pay by PayShap to a cellphone number, and time debit orders for the day money lands.
applies_when: you pay a monthly account fee, draw cash at ATMs, or have had a debit order bounce
not_when: you have no bank account and are paid in cash; the fee to look at then is the cost of carrying cash
steps: Open your banking app, find last month's statement, and write down every line that is a fee: monthly fee, ATM, declined debit order, SMS, deposit
Add them up: that total is what you paid last month just to use your own money
Circle the single biggest one; for most people it is either ATM withdrawals or a declined debit order fee
Replace that one habit this week: cash from the till at Pick n Pay, Boxer, Shoprite or Spar instead of the ATM, or PayShap instead of a branch EFT, or the debit order moved to the day after payday
Check your bank's fee guide in the app for the exact numbers, and compare it with GoTyme's published R0 monthly fee if you are thinking of moving
Never let a debit order bounce to 'save' money: the fee plus the retry costs more than the payment
cost: free to check; fees differ by bank and account, for example GoTyme publishes a R0 monthly fee and R3 for a declined debit order, confirm yours in your bank's app (checked 2026-10-30)

title: PayShap: send small amounts for free or nearly free
owner_summary: PayShap sends money instantly to someone's cellphone number (their ShapID) or account, and at most banks it is free or costs very little below R100, which is where most family and small payments sit. The fees differ by bank and change: TymeBank (now GoTyme) was reported as free at every amount, Nedbank and Capitec free or under R2 below R100, FNB and Standard Bank charging more above R100, so check your own bank's fee guide. Compared with an 'immediate payment' EFT, a cash-send voucher or a trip to deposit cash, it is the cheapest way to move money to a person. Pay in amounts under R100 where your bank's free rule allows it.
applies_when: you send money to family, pay someone by cellphone number, or pay a fee every time you transfer
not_when: the person you are paying has no bank account at all; a cash voucher or the till is the only route then
steps: Open your banking app, find 'PayShap' or 'Pay by cellphone number', and register your own ShapID (your cellphone number linked to your account)
Ask the person you pay to register theirs; a ShapID payment is often cheaper than one to an account number at the same bank
Look up your bank's PayShap fee in the app's fee guide: many banks charge R0 under R100, and the per-transaction limit differs (R3,000 at some banks, higher at others)
Send a test of R10 to a family member and check it arrives instantly
Move your regular small payments to PayShap: family money, a stokvel contribution, a share of groceries
Never pay a stranger by PayShap for goods you have not seen; it is instant and cannot be reversed
cost: free at some banks, up to about R7.50 a payment at others, mostly free or near-free under R100; fees are set by each bank and change, so confirm in your bank's fee guide (checked 2026-10-30)

keywords: save up or buy on account
title: Lay-by: the free way to buy on instalments
owner_summary: A lay-by is the one instalment plan that costs no interest: you pay the shop in parts and take the goods when it is paid. Under section 62 of the Consumer Protection Act your money stays yours until you take the goods, and if you cancel or cannot finish, the shop must refund you less a cancellation charge of at most 1% of the full price, and nothing at all if you stopped paying because of death or hospitalisation. A store account or furniture 'credit' is the opposite: interest, fees, and a listing on your credit record if you miss a payment. When you want something you cannot pay for today, lay-by first.
applies_when: you want to buy something over time, or you have a lay-by you cannot finish
not_when: you need the item today; a lay-by only works when you can wait until it is paid
steps: Ask the shop for a lay-by before you ask about an account: Pep, Ackermans, Jet and most furniture and clothing shops offer one
Get the agreement in writing: the full price, each instalment, the dates, and the cancellation charge (the law caps it at 1% of the full price)
Pay the instalments on payday from pot 1 and keep every receipt or SMS
If you cannot finish, cancel in writing and ask for your refund; the shop may keep at most 1% of the price, and nothing if the reason was death or hospital
If the shop refuses to refund, write to the National Consumer Commission or your provincial consumer office with the agreement and receipts; it is free
Never swap a lay-by for a store account to get the item sooner; the interest and the credit listing cost more than the wait
cost: free: no interest; a cancellation charge of at most 1% of the full price under Consumer Protection Act regulation 34 (checked 2026-10-30)

keywords: debit order i did not sign
title: Debit orders: approve them, time them, dispute the wrong ones
owner_summary: A debit order is permission for a company to take money from your account. Since DebiCheck, a new one must be approved by you in your banking app, by USSD or by phone before the first collection, so never approve one you do not recognise. Time every debit order for the day after money lands, so nothing bounces. If a debit order you did not agree to goes off, you can dispute and reverse it in the app: from 13 April 2026 the window across all debit order types is 60 calendar days, and after that it is a complaint to the company and the ombud. A DebiCheck debit that matches what you approved is very hard to reverse, so check the amount and date before you tap approve.
applies_when: debit orders go off your account, one has bounced, or you see one you do not recognise
not_when: you pay everything in cash or by manual transfer; there is nothing to dispute
steps: Open your banking app and list every debit order on the account under 'Debit orders' or 'DebiCheck'; write the company, amount and date for each
Move each date to the day after your money lands (ask the company; most change it by phone or app), so none bounce and you pay no declined fee
When a DebiCheck approval SMS arrives, check the company, amount and date against your list before you approve; decline anything you do not recognise
For a debit you never agreed to, dispute it in the app within 60 days of the debit (the rule since 13 April 2026); the bank reverses it and the company must prove you consented
Phone the company and cancel the agreement in writing the same day, or the debit returns next month
If the company keeps debiting, complain free to the National Financial Ombud on 0860 800 900; never close the account to escape a debit order, it follows you as a debt
cost: free to approve, move or dispute; the dispute window is 60 calendar days from 13 April 2026 (PASA rule change, checked 2026-10-30)

keywords: i buy things i don't need
title: The 24-hour rule for anything you did not plan
owner_summary: One rule stops most wasted money: anything that is not in the month plan waits 24 hours before you buy it. Not forever, just one night. Write it on a 'waiting' list in your notes app with the price. Most of the time the want fades by morning; when it does not, you buy it from pot 3 knowing what it replaces. The rule is strongest on payday weekend and at month-end specials, which is exactly when most unplanned money goes. It costs nothing and it is the single habit people who make the month fit have in common.
applies_when: money goes on things you did not plan, especially around payday or specials
not_when: the month plan has no room for anything unplanned at all; then the plan itself needs fixing, not the rule
steps: Make a page in your notes app called 'Waiting' and put the date next to it
When you want something that is not in the plan, write it there with the price instead of buying it
Wait 24 hours; do not go back to the shop or the link in that time
The next day, decide: if you still want it and pot 3 can carry it, buy it; if not, cross it out
On payday weekend and during specials like Black Friday, apply the rule to everything over the price of a loaf of bread
Once a month, read the crossed-out lines and add up what you did not spend; that number is why the rule works
cost: free

keywords: i don't know how much i owe
title: Write down everyone you owe, and what each one costs
owner_summary: You cannot pay down what you cannot see, and most people are paying whoever shouts loudest while the most expensive debt grows quietly. One list changes that: who, how much is left, what you pay a month, and the interest or fee. The cost is the column that matters: a mashonisa charging 30% to 50% a month goes to the top even if the amount is small, a store account next, a bank loan after. Ask each lender for a settlement balance; under the National Credit Act they must give it to you free. Then add up what goes out to all of them in a month. That number is the start of every debt plan.
applies_when: you owe money to more than one place, or you are not sure what you owe in total
not_when: you owe nobody; then the list is the cushion and the month plan
steps: Go through your SMSes, statements, the papers in the drawer and your banking app's debit orders, and write one line for every debt: bank, store account, cellphone contract, mashonisa, stokvel, family
Write 4 columns for each: how much is left, what you pay a month, the interest or fee, and the day it is due
Phone or message each lender for a settlement balance and the interest rate; the National Credit Act says they must give you a statement free of charge
Put the most expensive at the top: a mashonisa (often 30% to 50% a month) first, then store accounts, then bank loans, whatever the amounts
Add up the monthly payments: that total against your income tells you whether this is a snowball job or a debt review job
Keep the list where you see it on payday and update the balances every month; never add a new line to it
cost: free; a lender must give you a statement of your account free of charge under the National Credit Act; mashonisa interest is commonly reported at 30% to 50% a month (checked 2026-10-30)

title: Kill the smallest debt first: the snowball
owner_summary: Pay the minimum on every debt, on time, and send everything spare to one debt until it is gone: the mashonisa if there is one, otherwise the smallest balance. When it dies, add its whole payment to the next one. A study of about 6,000 people in debt programmes (Gal and McShane, Journal of Marketing Research 2012) found that closing accounts, however small, was the best predictor of clearing all the debt: the first win keeps you going. Highest-interest-first is better arithmetic, but most people quit it. Never take a 'consolidation loan' to do this; it is new credit with new fees, and the old habit comes back on top of it.
applies_when: you owe two or more debts and can cover all the minimums from your income
not_when: the minimums alone are more than the money; then debt review, not the snowball, is the route
steps: Take your owed list and write the balances in order, smallest at the top; a mashonisa goes to the very top whatever its size
Write the minimum payment next to each one, and circle the top one
On payday, pay every minimum first, in the order of the due dates, so nothing bounces
Send everything spare, even R50, to the circled debt the same day; do not touch the order when another one feels more urgent

For any lender you cannot pay in full, send one calm message with the amount and day you can pay: 'I can pay R300 on the 26th of each month until the balance is settled. Please confirm.' Keep the reply
When the top debt is paid, get the paid-up letter, cancel any insurance tied to it, and add its whole payment to the next one; never borrow to pay a debt
cost: free; the evidence is Gal and McShane 2012, about 6,000 people, closing small accounts first predicted paying everything off (checked 2026-10-30)

title: When a debt is paid: the letter, the insurance, the record
owner_summary: Paying the last instalment is not the end; three things make it stick. Ask the lender for a paid-up or settlement letter and keep it forever: it is your proof. Cancel any credit life insurance or 'account protection' tied to that account; under section 106 of the National Credit Act, if you paid the premium yearly you are owed the unused part back on settlement. Then check your credit report a month later: the account should show as settled, and a paid-up judgment must be removed by the bureau within 7 days of proof of payment under the 2014 regulations. If it still shows as owing, dispute it free with the bureau, letter attached.
applies_when: you have just made the last payment on a debt, or a paid account still shows as owing
not_when: the account is still open with a balance; this comes after the last instalment
steps: Ask the lender, in writing, for a paid-up or settlement letter showing a zero balance and the date; message or email so you have a copy
Check your bank app for any debit order still linked to that account (an insurance premium, a monthly fee) and cancel it with the company
Ask whether credit life insurance was charged on the loan; if you paid it yearly, section 106 of the National Credit Act gives you a refund of the unused part
Add the whole payment you were making to the next debt on your list the same payday
A month later, pull your free credit report and check the account shows 'settled' or 'closed'; a paid-up judgment must come off within 7 days of the bureau receiving proof
If it still shows as owing, lodge a dispute with the bureau with the letter attached; it is free and they have 20 business days; never pay a company to 'clear' it
cost: free: the letter, the dispute and the bureau update cost nothing; a paid-up judgment must be removed within 7 days of proof of payment (NCA regulations 2014, checked 2026-10-30)

title: What a mashonisa can and cannot do to you
owner_summary: Since 11 November 2016 anyone who lends money for interest must be registered with the National Credit Regulator, whatever the amount. A loan from an unregistered lender is an unlawful agreement under the National Credit Act, which means a court can declare it void and the lender cannot enforce it or its interest; and the NCR says holding your bank card, SASSA card, ID or PIN as security is a criminal offence. None of that makes the person go away, so the plan is quiet: pay a fixed amount on a fixed day, get your card and ID back, borrow nothing new, and report threats to the police. Report the lender to the NCR on 0860 627 627; it is free and they act on unregistered lenders.
applies_when: you owe a mashonisa, or one is holding your card, ID or PIN
not_when: the lender is registered with the NCR (ask for the NCRCP number and check it on ncr.org.za); then the normal NCA rules and caps apply
steps: Ask the lender for their NCR registration number (it starts NCRCP) and check it on ncr.org.za or by phoning 0860 627 627; no number means the agreement is unlawful under the National Credit Act
Write down what you borrowed, what you have paid so far and what they say you still owe; most people have already paid back more than they borrowed
If they hold your bank card, SASSA card, ID or PIN, ask once for it back; if they refuse, report it at the police station and to the NCR, because the NCR says holding it is a criminal offence
The moment the card is back, change the PIN in your banking app or at the bank, and check the account for withdrawals you did not make
Pay a fixed amount on a fixed day in a way that leaves a record (PayShap or a deposit slip), ask for the balance each time, and say no to any new loan
Never hand over a card, ID or PIN to anyone again, and report threats or intimidation to SAPS on 10111
cost: free to report; registration threshold for lenders is R0 since 11 November 2016 (Government Notice 513 of 2016), so every lender must be registered with the NCR (checked 2026-10-30)

keywords: should i go under debt review
title: Debt review: what it does, what it costs, what it stops
owner_summary: Debt review (section 86 of the National Credit Act) is a legal process for people whose repayments are more than they can pay. A registered debt counsellor tells your creditors, they must stop legal action while it runs, your payments are restructured into one lower amount, and when you finish you get a clearance certificate and the record is cleared. The catch: you cannot take any new credit while under review, and it costs money: an application fee of R50 and a restructuring fee that the NCR caps, with published figures of R8,000 (R9,000 if married in community of property) and an aftercare fee of 5% of the monthly payment capped at R400 or R450 depending on the source, so confirm the fee guideline on ncr.org.za before you sign. Most people who need it never use it, and many pay a scam for a worse version.
applies_when: your debt minimums are more than your income can carry, and lenders are threatening legal action
not_when: you can cover every minimum from your income; then the snowball clears it without fees or a listing
steps: Add up every monthly minimum on your owed list and compare it with your income after rent, food and transport; if the minimums do not fit, debt review is built for you

Read the cost before anything: R50 application fee, a restructuring fee capped by the NCR (published figures differ, R8,000 to R9,000, confirm on ncr.org.za), and a monthly aftercare fee of 5% of your payment with a cap
Understand the one thing it stops: no new credit of any kind until the clearance certificate, which for most people is the point
Find a counsellor registered with the NCR (the number starts NCRDC) and check it on ncr.org.za or on 0860 627 627; walk away from anyone who cannot show it

Sign Form 16 only after you have seen the fees in writing; within 5 business days the counsellor must send Form 17.1 to every creditor, and your payments then go through a registered payment distribution agent

Keep paying the restructured amount every month without fail; when the plan is done, the counsellor must issue the clearance certificate (Form 19) within 7 days, and never pay anyone extra to 'remove' you from review
cost: application fee R50; restructuring fee capped by the NCR, published figures differ (R8,000, R9,000 for couples in community of property); aftercare 5% of the monthly payment capped at R400 or R450 depending on the source; confirm on ncr.org.za (checked 2026-10-30)

keywords: fix my credit for a fee
remove bad credit for a fee
clear my name for a fee
title: Registered counsellor or removal scam: how to tell
owner_summary: There is no such thing as paying to have a true listing removed. Companies selling 'credit clearance', 'blacklisting removal' or 'debt review removal' for a fee are selling what the law already gives you free: a dispute with the bureau, a paid-up letter, a prescription defence, or a clearance certificate from your own counsellor. The NCR has warned (Circular 1 of 2024) about people using registered counsellors' numbers without permission, so the number alone is not enough; the name must match on the register. A real debt counsellor has an NCRDC number on ncr.org.za, puts fees in writing before Form 16, and never takes your payments into their own account.
applies_when: someone offers to clear your record, remove debt review or fix your credit for a fee
not_when: you are dealing with a counsellor whose NCRDC number and name you have already checked on ncr.org.za
steps: Ask for the NCRDC number in writing and check both the number and the name on the NCR register at ncr.org.za, or phone 0860 627 627; a CIPC company number is not registration
Refuse anyone who promises a 'guaranteed' clearance, asks for an upfront fee to remove a listing, or contacts you first on WhatsApp or Facebook
Ask the first-call questions: what are your fees in rand, who is the payment distribution agent, and how long until the court order; a real counsellor answers all three
Do for free what they charge for: dispute a wrong listing with the bureau (section 72), get the paid-up letter from the lender, or ask your counsellor for the clearance certificate (section 71)
If you already paid a removal company, stop further payments, keep the proof, and report them to the NCR on complaints@ncr.org.za
Never give anyone your banking login, OTP or ID copy to 'check your profile'; that is how the scam becomes identity theft
cost: free: disputes, paid-up letters, prescription and clearance certificates cost nothing; the NCR complaint line is 0860 627 627 (checked 2026-10-30)

keywords: they said they will take my furniture
title: Your rights when a debt collector calls
owner_summary: A debt collector must be registered with the Council for Debt Collectors; collecting without registration is a criminal offence under the Debt Collectors Act. They may ask you to pay; they may not threaten you, pretend to be a sheriff or a court, phone your employer or family about your debt, or add fees beyond the regulated tariff. Nobody can take your furniture without a court order served by a sheriff. Ask for the collector's registration number and the written breakdown of the debt, pay only what you agreed in writing, and complain free to the Council on 012 804 9808 or info@cfdc.org.za if they break the rules. If the debt is older than 3 years with no payment, do not acknowledge it before checking prescription.
applies_when: a collector, attorney or 'tracing agent' is phoning, messaging or sending letters about a debt
not_when: you have a court order against you; then the route is the court or a registered debt counsellor, not the Council
steps: Ask the caller for their name, the company, their Council for Debt Collectors registration number, and a written statement of the debt; a registered collector has all four
Check the number on the Council's register at cfdc.org.za or by phoning 012 804 9808; an unregistered collector is committing a crime and you need not deal with them
Check the date of the last payment on the debt: if more than 3 years ago with no acknowledgment, say nothing about owing it and read the prescribed-debt rules first
Pay only what you can, in writing: 'I can pay R200 on the 27th of each month. Confirm in writing and I will start.' Pay by a route that leaves a record
Keep a log of every call: date, time, name, what was said; threats, calls to your employer or family, or fake court documents go into a sworn complaint to the Council
Never pay cash to someone at your door and never give your card details over the phone; a collector is paid into the creditor's or their own registered account
cost: free to check the register and to complain; collector fees are set by the regulated tariff under the Debt Collectors Act, so ask for the breakdown (Council for Debt Collectors FAQ, checked 2026-10-30)

keywords: how much interest can they charge
they gave me a loan i couldn't afford
title: The interest caps, and what reckless lending means
owner_summary: The National Credit Act caps what a registered lender may charge. The published caps are: short-term credit (up to R8,000, repayable within 6 months) 5% a month on the first loan and 3% a month on another in the same year; unsecured loans the repo rate plus 21% a year; plus a capped initiation fee and a monthly service fee. A 2016 court case over the short-term caps was appealed, so confirm the current figures with the NCR. A lender must also check you can afford the loan before granting it (section 81); credit given without that check, or that you plainly could not afford, is reckless credit, and a court can set aside or suspend what you owe. This is a shield, not a reason to borrow: the caps still make small loans the most expensive money in the country.
applies_when: you are being charged interest or fees that look wrong, or you were given credit you could never afford
not_when: the lender is a mashonisa with no NCR number; then the whole agreement is unlawful, which is the stronger rule
steps: Read your credit agreement for three lines: the interest rate, the initiation fee and the monthly service fee; the lender must have given you a copy

Compare the rate with the caps: 5% a month (3% on a repeat loan in the same year) for short-term credit up to R8,000, and the repo rate plus 21% a year for unsecured loans; confirm the current numbers with the NCR on 0860 627 627
If the rate or fees are above the cap, write to the lender quoting the agreement and ask for the overcharge to be reversed; give them 20 business days

If a lender gave you credit without asking for payslips, bank statements or your other debts, or the instalment was more than you could ever pay, that is reckless credit under section 80; say so in writing
Lodge a free complaint with the NCR (form 29 on ncr.org.za, complaints@ncr.org.za) or with the National Financial Ombud on 0860 800 900 with the agreement and statements attached
Never take a new loan because the rate is 'within the cap'; the cap is the ceiling, not a good price
cost: free to complain; published caps are 5% a month (3% on a repeat loan) for short-term credit up to R8,000 and repo rate plus 21% a year for unsecured credit, under NCA regulation 42, with a 2016 court challenge to the short-term caps, so confirm with the NCR (checked 2026-10-30)

keywords: they are taking from my pay
title: A garnishee on your salary: what is legal
owner_summary: An emoluments attachment order (what people call a garnishee) lets a creditor take debt payments straight from your salary, but only if a magistrate's court granted it after deciding it is just and equitable; a clerk's stamp alone is not enough since the Constitutional Court's 2016 ruling and the 2017 law change. The total of all such orders may not exceed 25% of your basic salary. If more than that is coming off, or you never saw a court, your employer's payroll must show you the order and you can apply to the same court to have it set aside or reduced. Legal Aid South Africa helps with this free if you earn under its means test.
applies_when: money for a debt is being deducted from your salary, or a lender is threatening to 'garnish' you
not_when: the deduction is one you signed for yourself, like a payroll loan or a debit order; that is cancelled with the lender, not the court
steps: Ask your payroll or HR for a copy of the court order behind the deduction; they must have one, and it must be issued by a magistrate's court, not just signed by a clerk
Check two things on it: the court's name and the amount; if the total of all orders is more than 25% of your basic salary, it is above the legal cap
Write down what has been deducted so far from your payslips and compare it with the debt balance; orders sometimes run long after the debt is paid
If there is no proper court order, or it exceeds 25%, apply at that magistrate's court to set it aside or reduce it; the clerk of the civil court gives you the form
Phone Legal Aid South Africa's advice line or send a 'Please Call Me' to 079 835 7179; it is free if your income is under their means test (R9,400 a month for a single person from April 2026)
Never agree to a 'voluntary' salary deduction a lender puts in front of you to avoid court; it has none of the court's protections
cost: free to challenge through Legal Aid SA if you qualify; the legal cap is 25% of basic salary across all orders (Magistrates' Courts Act section 65J, checked 2026-10-30)

keywords: want money for an old account
title: Prescribed debt: after 3 years of silence, say nothing
owner_summary: Most ordinary debts (store accounts, cellphone contracts, personal loans, credit cards) prescribe after 3 years with no payment, no written acknowledgment and no summons. Section 126B of the National Credit Act, since March 2015, bars a creditor from collecting, selling or reactivating a prescribed credit-agreement debt. The trap is simple: if you acknowledge the debt in any way, by paying R10, by saying 'yes that's mine' on the phone, or by signing anything, the 3 years start again. So when a collector calls about an old account, ask for the date of the last payment in writing, and say nothing about owing it until you have checked. Home loans and SARS debts prescribe much later.
applies_when: a collector or lender contacts you about a debt you have not paid or heard about for 3 years or more
not_when: you paid, acknowledged or were served a summons within the last 3 years, or the debt is a home loan, a court judgment or tax
steps: Say only: 'Please send me the account details and the date of the last payment in writing.' Do not confirm the debt is yours on the phone
Check the last payment date on your own statements or your credit report; if it is more than 3 years ago with no summons and nothing signed, the debt has probably prescribed
Write back: 'This debt has prescribed under the Prescription Act and section 126B of the National Credit Act. I do not acknowledge it. Please stop collection.' Keep a copy
If it is still on your credit report, dispute it with the bureau as prescribed; the bureau has 20 business days and it is free
If the collector keeps going, complain to the NCR on 0860 627 627 or the National Financial Ombud on 0860 800 900 with your letter attached
Never pay 'just a little to make them stop' or sign an acknowledgment of debt on an old account; one payment restarts the 3 years
cost: free; ordinary debt prescribes after 3 years without payment, acknowledgment or summons (Prescription Act; NCA section 126B since March 2015), home loans and judgments much later (checked 2026-10-30)

keywords: new loan to pay old loan
title: Why a new loan never fixes old debt
owner_summary: A consolidation loan, a top-up, an overdraft, a credit card or a buy-now-pay-later plan all do the same thing: they add an initiation fee, a monthly service fee and interest to money you already owe, and they free up the old limits so the same habit fills them again. The National Credit Regulator's figures show more than a third of credit-active South Africans already behind; most got there one 'small' loan at a time. The rule in this plan is fixed: nothing new borrowed from anyone while the owed list exists. If the minimums truly do not fit, debt review is the legal route and costs less than another loan. If someone offers you credit, say the one line: 'Not while I am paying this off.'
applies_when: you are tempted by a consolidation loan, top-up, overdraft, credit card or buy-now-pay-later while you still owe money
not_when: you owe nobody and are not considering credit; nothing to decide
steps: Write down the full cost of the loan being offered, from its pre-agreement quote, which the lender must give you: initiation fee, monthly service fee, interest rate and the total you repay
Compare the total repayable with what you owe now; a consolidation that 'lowers the instalment' almost always raises the total and the years
Ask what happens to the old accounts: if they stay open, the limit is there to be used again, which is how the debt doubles
Say the one line to any offer, including a bank's app notification: 'Not while I am paying this off.' Tap 'not interested' and move on
If your minimums really do not fit your income, read the debt review entry; it is the legal version of what a consolidation loan pretends to be, with no new interest
Never take a loan from an app or a WhatsApp number; those are the most expensive and the least regulated
cost: free to refuse; a new loan adds an initiation fee, a monthly service fee and interest on top of what you owe, and the NCR reports more than 10 million credit-active consumers with impaired records (NCR June 2025, checked 2026-10-30)

keywords: how much should i have saved
how much should i be saving
title: Name the number: your first cushion target
owner_summary: Every mashonisa loan starts with a surprise: a funeral contribution, a school letter, a broken phone, a taxi fare to a clinic. A cushion is a named amount you can reach that turns the next surprise into a nuisance. Pick the first target from your own life, not from a rule: the cost of the last surprise, or one week of your essentials from the month plan. For most people that is a few hundred rand, and it is meant to be small; the person who cannot make one month does not need 'three months of salary' as a target, they need R500 they can reach. Write the number where you see it on payday. When you reach it, name the next one.
applies_when: you have nothing saved, or less than a week's spending you can reach
not_when: you already have more than a month's essentials saved; then the goal entry applies
steps: Write down the last 3 surprises that cost you money and what each one cost (the funeral contribution, the school shoes, the phone screen)
Pick the smallest of them, or one week of food and transport from your month plan, as the first target; round it to a number you can say, like R500
Write the number at the top of your month plan and in your notes app: 'Cushion: R500'
Open a separate place for it (a GoalSave or a savings pocket at your bank) so the everyday money cannot quietly eat it
Move the first amount today, however small, and set the rest to move on payday
When you reach the target, do not spend it on something planned; name the next number, and only use it for a real surprise
cost: free

title: Keep the cushion where the month cannot reach it
owner_summary: Savings in the same account as the groceries are not savings; they are next week's groceries. The fix is physical separation, which is what the rule-of-thumb research (Drexler, Fischer and Schoar 2014) found worked better than any training: a different pocket, a different account, a name on it. Most banks give you a free savings pocket inside the app: GoTyme's GoalSave pays interest from day 1 and more if you give 10 days' notice before taking it out, which is a useful speed bump. Interest is a bonus; the point is that you have to decide to take it out, instead of it going without you noticing.
applies_when: your savings keep getting spent because they sit with your everyday money
not_when: you have no bank account and no safe place at all; then a registered stokvel or burial society with written rules is the separate place
steps: Open your banking app and look for 'GoalSave', 'savings pocket', 'flexi savings' or 'notice savings'; at most banks it is free to open
Name it for what it is for ('Cushion') so you see the purpose every time you open the app
Move the first amount today, even R20, so the pocket exists before payday
If the bank offers a notice option (GoTyme's GoalSave pays more for 10 days' notice), choose it; the delay is the protection
Keep no card linked to the pocket and do not add it to your tap-to-pay; money that needs a transfer back is money you think about
Never keep the cushion as cash at home or on a card someone else holds; if you must use cash, a sealed envelope with a date on it is the minimum
cost: free: a savings pocket at your own bank costs nothing to open; GoTyme publishes 6% a year on GoalSave rising to 10% with 10 days' notice, confirm the current rates in the app (checked 2026-10-30)

title: Move it on payday, before you see it
owner_summary: Saving what is left at the end of the month saves nothing, because nothing is left. Saving on the day money lands, before the first spend, works because the decision is made once and the month adjusts around it. Set a recurring transfer in your banking app from your main account to the cushion for the day after payday: R50 on a grant, R200 on a salary, whatever the month plan says. The amount matters less than the day. In a month it truly cannot be afforded, pause the transfer for that month; never borrow to keep it going, and never cancel it altogether.
applies_when: you mean to save but there is never anything left by the time you try
not_when: your income is cash with no bank account; then the rule is the same but by hand: the first notes go into the envelope before anything is bought
steps: Decide the amount from your month plan, pot 2, and round it to a number that feels easy; the day is what matters
Open your banking app, choose the cushion pocket (GoalSave or your bank's savings pocket) and set a recurring transfer for the day after your money lands
Set a reminder on your phone for that day for the first 2 months, to check it moved
When income is a grant, set it for the grant date; when it is piece jobs, move it by hand the day you are paid, before you buy anything
In a month that is short, pause that month's transfer in the app; do not cancel the schedule, and do not borrow to cover it
After 3 paydays, raise it a little if the month fit, and never lower it just because the balance looks big
cost: free: a recurring transfer inside your own bank's app costs nothing at most banks, check the fee guide (checked 2026-10-30)

title: What the cushion is for, and how to refill it
owner_summary: The cushion has one job: to stop a surprise from becoming a loan. So the test for using it is simple: would you otherwise borrow for this? A funeral contribution, a clinic trip, a school letter, a broken stove: yes. A sale, a birthday, a new phone when the old one works: no, that goes on the waiting list. When you do use it, that is the cushion doing its job, not a failure. The week after, write the new balance, restart the payday transfer, and add anything you can until the number is back. Using it and refilling it a few times a year is exactly what a cushion is for.
applies_when: something has come up and you are deciding whether to use your savings or borrow
not_when: you have no cushion yet; then the question is the first target
steps: Ask the one question: 'If I did not have this money, would I borrow for this?' If yes, it is what the cushion is for; if no, it waits 24 hours on the waiting list
Take only what the surprise costs, not the whole pocket, and move it the day you need it
Write the new balance in your notes app with the date and what it was for
Restart the payday transfer the next payday; if you paused it for the surprise, unpause it
Add any extra that month (a refund, a small job) straight to the pocket until the number is back
Never borrow to 'protect' the cushion: paying 5% a month interest to keep R500 untouched costs more than using it
cost: free

title: GoalSave at GoTyme: how the pockets work
owner_summary: GoalSave is the savings pocket inside the GoTyme Bank app (the bank was TymeBank until January 2026). On its own GoalSave page GoTyme describes interest of 6% a year from day one and a bonus taking it to 10% a year if you give 10 days' notice before closing, with up to 20 GoalSaves and a combined cap of R250,000; third-party reviews describe a different ladder (4% rising to 6% after 90 days, then 10% with notice), so the exact tiers must be confirmed in the app before you count on them. There is no fee to open one. For a cushion, the notice option is the useful part: 10 days is long enough to stop a want and short enough for a real emergency.
applies_when: you bank with GoTyme or are opening an account there and want a separate place for savings
not_when: you bank elsewhere; use your own bank's savings pocket, the rule of separation is the same
steps: Open the GoTyme Bank app, tap 'Save' and choose 'GoalSave'; the account itself is free to open
Name the GoalSave for its purpose ('Cushion', 'School fees') and set the target amount from your month plan
Read the interest terms shown in the app at that moment: GoTyme's page describes 6% a year rising to 10% with 10 days' notice, but published figures differ, so the app is the source
Move the first amount today from your GoTyme account, and set a recurring transfer for the day after payday
When you need the money, choose the notice option if you can wait 10 days; immediate withdrawal is allowed but may lose the bonus interest
Never open a GoalSave with money you have borrowed to put in it; the interest is less than any loan costs
cost: free to open; GoTyme's own GoalSave page describes 6% a year rising to 10% a year with 10 days' notice, up to 20 GoalSaves and R250,000 in total; published figures differ, so confirm the tiers in the GoTyme app (checked 2026-10-30)

title: Your free credit report, once a year from every bureau
owner_summary: Section 72 of the National Credit Act gives you one free credit report a year from each registered credit bureau, so you can see exactly what lenders see: every account, every late payment, any judgment, and anything in your name that should not be. Get it on the bureau's own site with your own ID: TransUnion at transunion.co.za, Experian through its Up platform at up.experian.co.za, XDS through Splendi. Read it for three things: an account you do not recognise, a debt with no payment for 3 years that may have prescribed, and anything paid that still shows as owing. Each of those is a free dispute. Nobody, including this service, needs your ID number to do this; you type it on the bureau's site only.
applies_when: you have ever had an account, loan or contract in your name, or you were declined for credit and do not know why
not_when: you have never had any credit, account or contract; the bureau may have no file on you yet
steps: Go to transunion.co.za (free annual report page), up.experian.co.za or Splendi (XDS) on your phone and register with your own details; you will be asked for your ID number on their site, nowhere else
Answer the verification questions or the OTP they send, and download or view the report; online it is usually immediate
Read the accounts list and mark anything you do not recognise; that is possible fraud and goes to a dispute and SAFPS
Mark any account with no payment for 3 years and no summons; read the prescribed-debt rules before you touch it
Mark anything you have paid off that still shows a balance or 'adverse'; your paid-up letter is the evidence for a free dispute
Diary the date: you can get another free report from each bureau 12 months later, and never pay a site that charges for 'your free report'
cost: free: one report a year from each bureau under NCA section 72; TransUnion's call centre is 0861 482 482 if the site will not verify you (checked 2026-10-30)

title: Dispute what is wrong on your credit report, free
owner_summary: If something on your credit report is wrong, section 72 of the National Credit Act says the bureau must investigate it at no charge and resolve it within 20 business days of your challenge, and the NCR's guideline of December 2024 holds them to that. You dispute online on the bureau's own site or by email, with evidence: a paid-up letter, a statement showing the last payment was over 3 years ago, or an affidavit that an account is not yours. A listing that cannot be proved must come off. If the bureau ignores you or refuses, the complaint goes free to the National Credit Regulator or the National Financial Ombud. For an old debt, never pay a cent or acknowledge it before checking prescription; that restarts the 3 years.
applies_when: your report shows an account you do not recognise, an old debt, or something paid that still shows as owing
not_when: the listing is correct and current; then the fix is paying on time until it ages, not a dispute
steps: Write one line for each wrong item: the account, what the report says, and what is true, with the evidence next to it (paid-up letter, statement, bank letter, SAPS case number for fraud)
Lodge the dispute on the bureau's own site (TransUnion's 'dispute an item' page, Experian's Up platform, XDS's Splendi) or email, attaching the evidence; write the date down

Use plain words: 'I dispute the listing for [account]. It is [paid up on 12 March 2026 / not my account / prescribed, last payment June 2022]. Evidence attached. Please remove it under section 72 of the National Credit Act.'
Count 20 business days from the date you lodged; the bureau must have investigated and answered by then
If they refuse without proof, or do nothing, complain free to the NCR (complaints@ncr.org.za, 0860 627 627) or the National Financial Ombud on 0860 800 900, attaching your dispute and their reply
For an old debt, never pay 'to clear it' and never sign an acknowledgment while disputing; a wrong listing is removed for free, not bought off
cost: free; the bureau must investigate without charge and resolve within 20 business days (NCA section 72, NCR guideline December 2024, checked 2026-10-30)

keywords: how to get a good credit score
title: What actually moves your credit score
owner_summary: Your score is a summary of what the bureaus see: whether you pay on time, how much of your limits you use, how many accounts you have, and anything adverse. The one thing that moves it most is paying every account on the date, month after month; each bureau weighs things a little differently and scores on its own scale, so do not chase one number. What does not help: opening new accounts to 'build' a record (every application is a search against you, and it is new debt), paying a company to 'fix' it, or closing a settled account in anger. What does: set every payment to the day after payday so you cannot miss, keep store and card balances well below the limit, dispute what is wrong, and give it 3 clean months before you look again.
applies_when: you have been declined, your score is low, or you want a clean record before a big goal
not_when: you have never had credit and have no plans to; a score only matters when you need one
steps: Pull your free report from one bureau and write the accounts with their 'paid on time' history; that history, not the score, is what you are fixing
Set every account's payment to the day after your money lands, by DebiCheck or a scheduled payment, so no month is missed
Pay store cards and credit cards down to well under their limits and keep them there; high usage against the limit pulls the score down
Dispute anything wrong (free, 20 business days) and get paid-up letters for anything settled
Do nothing new: no new accounts, no 'credit builder' products, no applications, for 3 months; each one counts against you
After 3 months of every payment on the day, pull the report again from a different bureau (it is free) and compare; never pay a company that promises a score
cost: free; the bureaus' own guidance is that payment history weighs most and each bureau scores on its own scale (TransUnion 0 to 999), so compare history, not scores (checked 2026-10-30)

keywords: how long does a judgment stay
title: A paid judgment must come off within 7 days
owner_summary: If a court judgment was granted against you and you have since paid it, you do not need a lawyer to clear it. Under the 2014 regulations on the removal of adverse consumer credit information, the creditor must send proof of payment to every registered bureau within 7 days of receiving it, and the bureau must remove the paid-up judgment within 7 days of receiving that proof; the bureaus must then tell each other within 3 days. The creditor may never relist it. Paid-up defaults are removed once the lender confirms paid-up status. So the move is: pay it, get the paid-up letter, send the letter to the bureaus yourself, and dispute if it is still there after a few weeks.
applies_when: a judgment or default on your credit report has been paid in full
not_when: the judgment is unpaid; then it is a debt to settle or arrange, and a registered debt counsellor or Legal Aid SA can advise on rescission
steps: Pay the judgment debt in full and ask the creditor or their attorney for a paid-up letter the same day, with the case number on it
Ask the creditor to send proof of payment to all registered bureaus; the regulations give them 7 days
Send the paid-up letter yourself to TransUnion, Experian and XDS through their dispute channels, so you are not waiting on the creditor
Count 7 days from when the bureau received it; the judgment must be removed, and the other bureaus informed within 3 days
Pull your free report after 3 weeks; if the judgment or the paid default still shows, lodge a section 72 dispute with the letter attached
Never pay a 'judgment removal' company; the removal is the bureau's legal duty and costs nothing
cost: free; creditor sends proof within 7 days, bureau removes within 7 days of receiving it, other bureaus within 3 days (Removal of Adverse Consumer Credit Information Regulations 2014, checked 2026-10-30)

keywords: debt review on my credit report
can i get credit after debt review
title: Finishing debt review: the clearance certificate
owner_summary: Debt review ends with a clearance certificate (Form 19), not just the last payment. Section 71 of the National Credit Act says your debt counsellor must issue it within 7 days of you satisfying the restructured plan, and within a further 7 days must file a copy with every registered credit bureau, which must then expunge the debt review record. If the counsellor drags their feet, you can apply to the National Consumer Tribunal. Until the certificate is filed, the flag stays and no lender may give you credit, so chase it in writing on the day of the last payment. The certificate is yours by law; never pay a 'removal' company for it.
applies_when: you have made the last payment under a debt review plan, or paid up everything except a home loan that is current
not_when: you still have restructured debts with balances; the certificate only comes when the plan is satisfied
steps: On the day of the last restructured payment, message your debt counsellor: 'All restructured debts are paid. Please issue my clearance certificate (Form 19) under section 71 within 7 days.' Keep the message
Ask the payment distribution agent for a final statement showing every account at zero; attach it
Count 7 days; the counsellor must have issued the certificate, and 7 days after that it must be filed with all the bureaus
Pull your free credit report after 3 weeks and check the debt review flag is gone; if not, dispute with the bureau attaching the certificate
If the counsellor refuses or stalls, complain to the NCR on 0860 627 627 or apply to the National Consumer Tribunal; both are free
Never take new credit in the first months after clearance just because you can; the cushion comes first
cost: free; the counsellor must issue the certificate within 7 days and file it with the bureaus within a further 7 days (NCA section 71, NCR guideline February 2026, checked 2026-10-30)

title: Funeral cover: the rules that decide whether it pays
owner_summary: A funeral policy is the cheapest protection a household can buy, and the one most often sold badly. The rules to know: most policies have a waiting period of up to 6 months for death from natural causes (some insurers 3 months), while accidental death is usually covered from day one; if you already served a waiting period on another funeral policy, the new insurer may not make you serve it again. You have a cooling-off period of 31 days after getting the policy documents to cancel and get your money back if you have not claimed. A missed premium can lapse the policy, so pay it the day after money lands. Before you sign, check the insurer or its underwriter is licensed with the FSCA.
applies_when: you are buying, holding or claiming on a funeral policy, or paying one you do not understand
not_when: you have no dependants and someone else already covers your own funeral in writing
steps: Read the policy schedule for 4 things: who is covered, the payout amount, the monthly premium, and the waiting period for natural death
Check the insurer's name on the FSCA register at fsca.co.za or by phoning 0800 110 443; an unlicensed 'funeral scheme' pays nobody
If you had a funeral policy before, tell the new insurer in writing; under the Policyholder Protection Rules they may not impose a new waiting period you have already served
Set the premium debit order for the day after money lands; a lapsed policy means a new waiting period
If you change your mind, cancel within 31 days of receiving the documents and the premiums must be refunded if you have not claimed

When claiming, send the death certificate and the claim form the same week and ask for the insurer's written decision; if it is rejected unfairly, the National Financial Ombud on 0860 800 900 takes the complaint free
cost: the premium is set by the insurer; the rules that protect you are free: up to 6 months waiting for natural death, accidental death usually from day 1, 31 days cooling-off (FSCA guidance, Policyholder Protection Rules, checked 2026-10-30)

keywords: paying for the same thing twice
title: One policy that fits; cancel the doubles
owner_summary: Most households are paying for the same funeral twice: a policy from a shop account, one through a grant deduction, a burial society, and the one the family took out years ago. Only one will be needed, and the rest are money thrown away every month. List every policy, society and plan with its premium, its payout, who it covers and its waiting period. Keep the one with the best payout per rand of premium that covers the people who actually depend on you, and whose waiting period you have already served. Cancel the doubles in writing, and watch for the grant: SASSA allows only one funeral deduction, and it may never be more than 10% of the grant.
applies_when: you pay more than one funeral policy, society or plan, or you are not sure what you are paying for
not_when: you have exactly one policy that covers everyone who depends on you
steps: Write every policy, burial society and plan on one page: the name, the monthly premium, the payout, who it covers, and the waiting period left
Check your bank statement and your grant statement for premiums you forgot: a policy sold with a store account, a cellphone 'cover', a deduction on a grant
Divide each payout by its premium: the one that pays most per rand, covers the right people, and has served its waiting period is the one to keep
Cancel the doubles by phone and then in writing: 'Please cancel policy number [x] from [date] and confirm in writing.' Keep the confirmation and watch next month's statement
For a policy deducted from a SASSA grant you did not agree to, dispute it by SMS to 34548 with your ID number and the insurer's name, and cancel with the insurer
Never cancel the policy you are keeping to 'start fresh'; a new policy means a new waiting period of up to 6 months
cost: free to cancel; the saving is every double premium; a SASSA grant may carry only one funeral deduction of at most 10% (checked 2026-10-30)

title: Name who gets it, and tell them where the papers are
owner_summary: A policy pays the person named on it, not the person who needs it. If the beneficiary is nobody, an ex-partner, or someone who has died, the payout goes into your estate and your family waits months while the Master of the High Court sorts it out. Check every policy, funeral plan, bank account and retirement fund for the named beneficiary, change it on the insurer's or fund's form where it is wrong, and tell that person two things: that the policy exists and where the papers and the policy number are. For a retirement fund the trustees decide according to who depended on you, but your nomination form guides them. A simple will, kept with the papers, finishes the job.
applies_when: someone depends on your income, and you have any policy, fund or account
not_when: you have no policy, no fund and no account; then the first job is the one policy that fits
steps: List every policy, fund and account you have, and next to each write who is named as the beneficiary; phone the insurer or fund if you do not know
Change any that are wrong on the insurer's or fund's own beneficiary form; most accept it by email or in the app, and it is free
For a provident or pension fund, fill in the fund's nomination form naming everyone who depends on you; the trustees use it under section 37C of the Pension Funds Act
Tell the beneficiary, in person, that the policy exists, the insurer's name, the policy number and where the papers are kept
Put the papers (or photos of them) in one place: a folder at home and a copy on your phone or email
Write a simple will naming who gets what, sign it in front of 2 witnesses who are not beneficiaries, and keep it with the papers; never leave it to 'the family will know'
cost: free: changing a beneficiary with the insurer or fund costs nothing; a basic will can be written yourself and witnessed by 2 people (checked 2026-10-30)

title: The bank never asks for your PIN, OTP or app approval
owner_summary: SABRIC's 2025 report counted R2.41 billion stolen through digital banking, 88.6% of it through banking apps, and almost none of it by hacking: people were talked into it by someone pretending to be the bank, the police or a courier. Three facts stop most of it. The bank never phones to ask for your PIN, password, OTP or to approve something in the app; a real bank call never needs those. A SIM swap starts with your phone losing signal for no reason; if that happens, phone your network and your bank's fraud line from another phone immediately. And no OTP is ever shared with anyone, including family, because the OTP is the money. Switch on every security setting in your app and keep the fraud number saved.
applies_when: you use a banking app, get bank SMSes, or someone has phoned claiming to be from the bank
not_when: you have no bank account at all; then the risk is cash and the SASSA card PIN, same rule: tell nobody
steps: Open your banking app's security settings and switch on every lock: app PIN or fingerprint, transaction notifications, card lock, and limits on online and international purchases

Save your bank's fraud line in your phone now (Capitec 0860 10 20 43, FNB 087 575 9444, Standard Bank 0800 222 050, Absa 0860 557 557, Nedbank 0800 110 929, GoTyme 0860 999 119) and confirm it against the number in your app, never from an SMS
If your phone loses signal for no reason, treat it as a SIM swap: phone your network from another phone, then the bank's fraud line, and ask them to block the account
If anyone phones 'from the bank' asking for a PIN, OTP, password or to approve an app message to 'stop fraud', hang up and call the bank's number from your card yourself
Never click a link in an SMS or WhatsApp to 'verify', 'unlock' or 'claim a refund'; open the app yourself instead
If money has gone: fraud line first, then the police case number, then SAFPS protective registration; all three are free
cost: free: every app security setting and every fraud line is free; SABRIC reported R2.41 billion in digital banking losses in 2025, 88.6% through banking apps (checked 2026-10-30)

keywords: pay a fee for a job
title: Check any offer before a cent moves
owner_summary: A real investment is licensed and boring; a scheme is urgent and exciting. The signs are the same every time: returns that are 'guaranteed' or far above what a bank pays, pressure to recruit friends to earn, paying in to 'unlock' a payout, a job that asks for a registration fee, and a contact that only exists on WhatsApp or Telegram. Under section 43 of the Consumer Protection Act, any scheme offering a return 20 percentage points or more above the repo rate is a multiplication scheme and illegal to promote or join. Before any money moves, check the company and its FSP number on the FSCA's register at fsca.co.za or on 0800 110 443, and check the name matches the number; scammers borrow real FSP numbers.
applies_when: someone offers you an investment, a trading group, a 'stokvel' with returns, or a job that needs a fee
not_when: the money is going to a bank savings product or a fund whose FSP number you have already matched on the FSCA register
steps: Ask for the company's registered name and FSP number in writing, and the name of the person's own licence
Search both on the FSCA register at fsca.co.za (or phone 0800 110 443) and check the name on the register matches the name you were given; a borrowed number is the commonest trick
Run the 5 signs: guaranteed returns, recruit-to-earn, pay-to-get-paid, a job that charges a fee, WhatsApp or Telegram only; one sign is enough to stop
Do the arithmetic: 20 percentage points above the repo rate is a multiplication scheme under section 43 of the Consumer Protection Act, and anything promising 30% a month is a scheme by definition
Say the one line and leave: 'Send me the FSP number and I will check it.' Real providers are glad to; schemes argue
