If you already paid, stop paying, keep every message, report it to the FSCA and the police, and warn the person who recruited you; never pay more to 'release' your money
cost: free to check: the FSCA register and its line 0800 110 443 cost nothing; a return 20 percentage points above the repo rate is an illegal multiplication scheme under CPA section 43 (checked 2026-10-30)

title: Protective registration with SAFPS: free, and it works
owner_summary: If your ID, passport, driver's licence or phone is lost or stolen, or someone has opened an account in your name, register with the Southern African Fraud Prevention Service. Protective Registration is free: SAFPS puts a marker against your identity so that when anyone applies for credit, a contract or an account in your name, the member bank or lender gets an alert and must check it is really you. You apply on safps.org.za, by email to protection@safps.org.za with a certified copy of your ID and the form, or by phone on 011 867 2234, and you get a reference number within about 48 hours. It does not block you from getting credit yourself; it only makes the lender check harder. Do it the same day the ID goes missing.
applies_when: your ID or phone is lost or stolen, you have shared your ID copy with someone you do not trust, or there is an account you did not open
not_when: nothing has been lost and nothing strange is on your credit report; it is still free, but the report check comes first
steps: Report the lost or stolen ID at the police station and get the case number; SAFPS and the bank will ask for it
Go to safps.org.za, choose 'Apply for Protective Registration', and fill in the form; or email the form with a certified ID copy to protection@safps.org.za, or phone 011 867 2234
Keep the reference number SAFPS sends (usually within 48 hours) with your police case number
If a lender already gave credit in your name, ask them in writing for a letter confirming impersonation; with that letter SAFPS can list you as a victim of impersonation too
Pull your free credit report from each bureau and dispute any account that is not yours, attaching the case number and the SAFPS reference
Never post a photo of your ID on WhatsApp groups or hand a copy to a 'job agent'; a copy is all a fraudster needs
cost: free: Protective Registration costs nothing and a reference number is issued within about 48 hours (SAFPS, checked 2026-10-30)

keywords: how to say no to family
title: Set the family line: one amount, one day
owner_summary: Helping family is not the problem; helping without a number is, because it is the line in your month that changes every time the phone rings, and it is usually the line that pushes a month into a loan. The fix is one fixed amount, sent on the same day every month by PayShap, said once and kindly: the amount, the day, and that it will come every month so they can plan around it. The amount comes from your month plan after bills and the money put aside, not from the last request. When an extra request comes, the answer is one line: 'That will have to wait for next month's amount.' It protects them as much as you: a fixed amount that arrives beats a bigger one that sometimes does not.
applies_when: family or relatives regularly ask for money and the amount changes every month
not_when: nobody outside your household depends on you, or the family amount is already fixed and sent on a set day
steps: Write down what you actually gave to family in each of the last 3 months, from your banking app and your memory; the real number is usually higher than you think
Look at your month plan: after pot 1 (bills) and pot 2 (cushion), what can the month carry every month without a loan? That is the family line
Choose the day: the day after your money lands, by PayShap to their ShapID, so it arrives before the asking starts
Say it once, in a calm moment, not when someone asks: 'From now on I send R[amount] on the [day] every month. It will always come. Extra requests will have to wait for the next month.'
Write it in the month plan as its own line, and send the same amount on the same day for 3 months so people can plan around it
When an extra request comes, use the one line and do not borrow to meet it; never cut the amount in anger, and never raise it because the asking got louder
cost: free; a PayShap payment under R100 is free at most banks, and sending on one day replaces several transfers (checked 2026-10-30)

title: Check the stokvel you pay into
owner_summary: More than 11 million South Africans belong to a stokvel, and a good one is the oldest cushion there is. A safe one has four things: a written constitution that says who the members are, how much and when you pay, how and when payouts happen, and what happens when someone leaves; a bank account in the stokvel's name needing two or three signatures, not the treasurer's personal account; books any member can see; and, for bigger groups, registration with NASASA, which has a sample constitution and a line on 010 007 2129. A 'stokvel' that promises returns, pays you for recruiting, or needs you to pay in before you can take out is not a stokvel; it is a pyramid scheme, and illegal.
applies_when: you pay into a stokvel, burial society or savings club, or are thinking of joining one
not_when: you belong to none; then this is a check for the future before you join one
steps: Ask for the constitution and read it for 4 things: members, contributions and dates, how payouts are decided, and what happens when someone leaves or dies
Ask where the money sits: a bank account in the stokvel's name needing 2 or 3 signatures is safe; cash with the treasurer or a personal account is not
Ask to see the books or the bank statement at the next meeting; every member has the right to look
Check whether the group is registered with NASASA (phone 010 007 2129 or email info@nasasa.co.za), and use NASASA's sample constitution if yours has none
Test it against the pyramid signs: promised returns, money for recruiting, paying in to 'unlock' a payout; any one of them, leave
Never pay a contribution in cash without a signed receipt in the book, and never hand your bank card or PIN to the treasurer 'for convenience'
cost: free to check; NASASA (010 007 2129) offers a sample constitution, and more than 11 million South Africans belong to a stokvel (NASASA 2025, checked 2026-10-30)

title: Burial society or funeral policy: what each one really pays
owner_summary: A burial society pays from the members' own pool, in cash or in kind (the tent, the coffin, the cooking), decided by its own rules; a funeral policy pays a fixed amount from a licensed insurer under the Policyholder Protection Rules, with a waiting period and a cooling-off right. Neither is better; the mistake is paying both for the same funeral, or trusting a society or a parlour 'scheme' with no written rules. Ask the society what exactly it pays, in writing, and whether its money sits in a bank account with more than one signature. Ask a funeral parlour selling cover for the name of the licensed insurer behind it and check it on the FSCA register; a parlour is not an insurer.
applies_when: you pay into a burial society, a parlour scheme, or both a society and a policy
not_when: you have one funeral policy with a licensed insurer and no society; then the policy list is the check
steps: Write what the society promises to pay and in what form (cash, coffin, tent, groceries), from its constitution or minutes, not from memory
Ask the treasurer where the money is kept: a bank account in the society's name with 2 or 3 signatures, with the statement shown at meetings
For a parlour or 'scheme', ask for the underwriter's name and FSP number and check it on fsca.co.za or on 0800 110 443; no licensed insurer means no legal cover
Put the society and every policy on one page with premium, payout and who is covered, and keep the combination that covers the family once, not twice
If the society's rules are only in someone's head, propose adopting NASASA's sample constitution at the next meeting
Never stop a licensed policy to rely only on a society whose books you have not seen, and never pay a parlour in cash without a receipt and a policy document
cost: free to check; a society's payout is set by its own rules, a policy's by the schedule; the FSCA line 0800 110 443 confirms whether an insurer is licensed (checked 2026-10-30)

keywords: take out a loan for a friend
account in my name for someone
take a contract for my cousin
title: Lending to family: give it, write it, or say no
owner_summary: Money lent to family is usually a gift with a grudge attached. The rule is three choices and nothing in between: give it if you can afford to never see it again; lend it in writing, with the amount, the date and how it comes back, if you cannot; or say no with the one line. Never do the fourth thing: putting your own name on their debt, by taking a loan, a cellphone contract or a store account for someone else, or signing surety. The lender does not know or care whose phone it is; the listing, the collectors and the garnishee come to you, and a family promise is no defence. The National Credit Act protects borrowers from lenders, not from each other.
applies_when: a relative or friend asks you to lend money, take credit in your name, or sign for them
not_when: nobody is asking and your month plan already has the fixed family line
steps: Decide which of the 3 it is before you answer: a gift from pot 3 you can afford, a written loan, or a no
For a loan, write it on paper or in a WhatsApp message both of you keep: 'I lend you R400 on 3 November 2026. You pay R100 on the 27th of each month until it is paid.' A message is a record
Choose a repayment day that is their payday, not yours, and remind once, kindly, the day before
Say no to any request to open an account, take a contract or sign surety in your name with the one line: 'I don't put my name on anyone's debt, not even family.'
If you already have, get the account statement from the lender, pay the arrears yourself to protect your record, and cancel or transfer the account as soon as the contract allows
Never lend what you would have to borrow to replace, and never hand over your bank card to 'help out'
cost: free; a written note or a WhatsApp message both keep is enough to record a loan between people (checked 2026-10-30)

title: A 'stokvel' that pays returns is a pyramid scheme
owner_summary: Every few years the pyramid scheme comes back wearing a stokvel's clothes: a 'gifting circle', a 'blessing loom', a 'community investment' on WhatsApp or Facebook where you pay in and get paid when others join. Section 43 of the Consumer Protection Act makes it illegal to promote or take part in a pyramid scheme (payouts come from recruiting, not from anything sold), a chain letter, or a multiplication scheme (a promised return 20 percentage points or more above the repo rate). The National Consumer Tribunal fined Up Money R1 million for exactly this. The last people in always lose, and they are usually family. A real stokvel pays out what the members put in, in turn, and nothing more.
applies_when: someone invites you to a group that pays out when you recruit, or a 'stokvel' promising a return on what you pay in
not_when: the group is a rotating or grocery stokvel with a constitution, where payouts are the members' own contributions in turn
steps: Ask the one question: 'Where does the payout money come from?' If the answer is new members, it is a pyramid scheme under section 43 of the Consumer Protection Act
Do the arithmetic on any promised return: paying R500 to receive R4,000 is a multiplication scheme, illegal whatever it is called
Check the signs: recruit-to-earn, pay to 'unlock' your payout, WhatsApp or Facebook only, pressure to join 'before it closes'
Say no to the person who invited you with one line: 'I only put money where I can see the constitution and the bank statement.'
If you have paid in, stop, keep every message and proof of payment, and report it to the National Consumer Commission; the Tribunal has fined schemes like Up Money R1 million
Never recruit someone else to get your own money back; that makes you the one breaking the law, and it is usually family who loses
cost: free to walk away; promoting or joining a pyramid or multiplication scheme (20 percentage points above the repo rate) is prohibited under CPA section 43, and Up Money was fined R1 million (checked 2026-10-30)

title: Match the goal to the place the money lives
owner_summary: Money without a destination drifts back into the month. Once the cushion exists, each bigger goal needs a vehicle that fits how far away it is. Within a year: a savings pocket or GoalSave at your bank, where the money is reachable. Several years away: a tax-free savings account, where the growth is never taxed, up to R46,000 a year from 1 March 2026 and R500,000 in a lifetime. A first home: the First Home Finance subsidy through the NHFC if your household earns R3,501 to R22,000 a month. Retirement: the fund you already have at work, left alone. The vehicle decides nothing about the amount; the goal sentence does that. One goal, one vehicle, one automatic transfer on payday.
applies_when: the cushion is in place and you are saving toward something with a number and a date
not_when: you have no cushion yet or you still owe a mashonisa; the cushion and the owed list come before any goal
steps: Write the goal in one sentence with a number and a date: 'R12,000 for Thabo's school fees by January 2028'
Count the months to the date and divide: that is the monthly number, and it has to fit pot 2 of the month plan

Pick the vehicle by distance: under a year, a GoalSave or savings pocket at your bank; more than 3 years, a tax-free savings account (R46,000 a year, R500,000 lifetime); a first home, the NHFC First Home Finance subsidy if your household earns R3,501 to R22,000 a month
Open it with a provider you can check on the FSCA register, and name it for the goal
Set a recurring transfer for the day after payday for the monthly number, and nothing else touches it
Never fund a goal by withdrawing retirement savings or taking credit; a goal that costs interest or your pension is not a goal, it is a debt
cost: free to set up at most banks; tax-free savings allow R46,000 a year from 1 March 2026 and R500,000 in a lifetime (SARS), and First Home Finance covers household incomes of R3,501 to R22,000 a month (NHFC, checked 2026-10-30)

title: Tax-free savings: the rules that bite
owner_summary: A tax-free savings account grows without any tax on the interest or growth, which is why it is the right place for a goal 3 years or more away. From 1 March 2026 you may put in up to R46,000 a tax year (R36,000 before), across all your tax-free accounts together, and R500,000 in your lifetime. Anything over either limit is taxed at 40% by SARS, so one accidental extra deposit costs real money. Withdrawing is allowed at any time, but what you take out does not restore the room: the lifetime count only goes up. So use it only for money you will not need soon, start small, and let the yearly limit be the ceiling, not the target.
applies_when: you have a cushion and are saving for something 3 or more years away
not_when: you are still building the cushion or paying expensive debt; a tax-free account is for money you will not touch
steps: Open a tax-free savings account with a bank, unit trust company or investment platform you have checked on the FSCA register; the account must be labelled 'tax-free' under SARS rules
Decide the monthly number from your goal sentence; it may be small, there is no minimum in the law
Set a recurring transfer for the day after payday and stay well under R46,000 a year across all your tax-free accounts (the limit from 1 March 2026)
Keep a running total in your notes app of everything you have ever paid in; the lifetime limit of R500,000 counts deposits, not the balance
Do not withdraw for anything except the goal; money taken out never gives you the contribution room back
Never pay in more than the limits, even by mistake: SARS taxes the excess at 40%, and never open a second one without counting the first
cost: free to open at most providers (fees differ, ask); annual limit R46,000 from 1 March 2026, lifetime R500,000, excess taxed at 40% (SARS, checked 2026-10-30)

keywords: government help to buy a house
title: First Home Finance: the subsidy for a first home
owner_summary: First Home Finance (the programme once called FLISP) is a once-off government subsidy toward buying a first home, for South African citizens and permanent residents whose household earns R3,501 to R22,000 a month, who have never owned property or had a housing subsidy, and who will live in the home. The subsidy is bigger the lower your income; published figures for 2026 differ (a top of R169,264, a bottom of R27,960 or R38,878), so use the NHFC's calculator for your own number. It pays toward the deposit or reduces the home loan. Applications go through the NHFC's online portal, which opens in windows, or through a participating bank when you apply for the loan.
applies_when: you want to buy a first home, have a steady income in the band, and have never owned property
not_when: your household income is above R22,000 or below R3,501 a month, you have owned property before, or you already received a housing subsidy
steps: Check the 4 conditions: household income R3,501 to R22,000 a month, first-time buyer, citizen or permanent resident, and you will live in the home
Use the NHFC First Home Finance calculator on nhfc.co.za with your income to see your subsidy; published ranges differ, so trust the calculator, not a blog
Get your credit record clean first: a home loan needs 3 months of on-time payments on everything, so this goal starts in the credit-record part of your plan
Get a home loan approval in principle from a bank and tell them you intend to apply for First Home Finance; some banks still ask for the approval first

Apply on the NHFC online portal during an open window (the portal closes between windows, so check nhfc.co.za) with your ID, payslips or bank statements and the loan quote; never through a third party who charges a fee
Never sign an offer to purchase before the subsidy and the loan are both confirmed in writing
cost: free to apply; household income band R3,501 to R22,000 a month; published 2026 subsidy figures differ (up to R169,264), so confirm on the NHFC calculator (checked 2026-10-30)

keywords: how much tax on two pot
should i withdraw my two pot
take money out of my pension
title: Two-pot: what a withdrawal costs you
owner_summary: Since 1 September 2024 a third of each new retirement contribution goes into a savings pot you can reach before retirement. You may take one withdrawal from it per tax year, at least R2,000, through your fund's own portal, and it is taxed at your marginal rate with no tax-free portion, and SARS deducts any tax you already owe before it pays. Once paid, it cannot be reversed or paid back in. It is your money, and in a real emergency it is better than a mashonisa; but every rand taken is a rand that will not be there at 60, and the tax alone usually costs more than the cushion would have. In this plan the order is fixed: cushion first, two-pot only for a true emergency, and never for a goal.
applies_when: you belong to a pension, provident or retirement annuity fund and are thinking of taking from the savings pot
not_when: you have no retirement fund, or your need can be met from the cushion
steps: Ask yourself the cushion question first: would you borrow for this? If not, it does not come out of the savings pot
Log in to your fund administrator's two-pot portal (your HR or the fund's member line has the link) and read your savings pot balance; do not guess
Work out the tax: the amount is added to your income for the year and taxed at your marginal rate, with no tax-free portion, and SARS first deducts any tax debt
Remember the rules: one withdrawal per tax year (1 March to 28 February), minimum R2,000, and it cannot be cancelled once the tax directive is issued
If you do withdraw, take only what the emergency costs, and put the rest of the plan back on payday the next month
Never withdraw to pay a 'quick' debt you could snowball, and never for a goal; a goal has its own vehicle
cost: no fee from most funds, but the withdrawal is taxed at your marginal rate with no tax-free portion; one per tax year, minimum R2,000, cannot be reversed (SARS and fund guidance, checked 2026-10-30)

keywords: how much to save a month
title: The goal sentence: a number, a date, a monthly amount
owner_summary: A goal you cannot say in one sentence will not get saved for. Write it as: what, how much, by when. Find the real cost from a quote, a letter from the school, or last year's receipt, never a guess. Count the months to the date and divide: that is the monthly number. If it does not fit pot 2 of your month plan, move the date, not the plan; a goal that needs a loan at the end is not a goal. Then automate it on payday into the vehicle that fits. The December-and-January trap catches most households: school fees, uniforms and the holiday arrive together, so that goal starts in February, not November.
applies_when: you have something you want to pay for in the next year or two and no number for it yet
not_when: you have no cushion and expensive debt; the goal waits until those are handled
steps: Write what the goal is in one line, like 'school fees and uniform for January 2027'
Find the real cost: ask the school for the fee letter, get a quote, or take last year's receipt; write the number
Count the months between now and the date, and divide the cost by the months; that is the monthly number
Check it against pot 2 of the month plan; if it does not fit, move the date further out or lower the cost, never borrow the difference
Open or name a GoalSave or savings pocket for it and set the monthly number to move the day after payday
Never raid it for a want, and never plan the big January goal to start in November; start it in February and the month never feels it
cost: free

title: Money with a partner: who pays what, and what is yours
owner_summary: Decide together, once, who pays which bills, in writing, and keep one account each for your own money even if you also share one. Fair is not always half-half: splitting the shared bills in the same proportion as what each of you earns leaves both of you with something. If you are married, your marriage contract decides who owns what and who answers for whose debts, and that matters more than whose name is on the account. If you do not know how you are married, or your partner is hiding money or running up debt in both your names, Legal Aid SA gives free advice to people who qualify, and nobody there is selling anything.
applies_when: you live with a partner and the bills, the accounts or the debts are shared or argued about
not_when: you are single, or the question is about family outside your own household (see the family line)
steps: Write every household bill in one list with who pays it now
Agree one way to split the shared bills, in the same proportion as what each of you brings in, and write it down
Keep one account each for your own money; if you share an account, it holds only the shared bills
Find out how you are married (your marriage certificate or the contract says), because that decides whose debt is whose
If money is being hidden or debt made in your name, ask Legal Aid SA whether you qualify for free advice before you sign anything
cost: Free; Legal Aid SA advice is free for people who qualify
stakes: A debt made in a joint estate is both of yours; a shared account with no rules is the commonest money fight

title: Child maintenance: the court does it free, no lawyer needed
owner_summary: A child's other parent must help pay for the child, and you do not need a lawyer or any money to make it happen. The maintenance office at your nearest magistrate's court takes the application free, calls the other parent in, and the court can order a fixed monthly amount and, if it is not paid, have it taken straight from their salary. Bring your ID, the child's birth certificate, proof of what the child costs you each month, and whatever you know about where the other parent works. It takes time, so start now rather than waiting for a promise.
applies_when: the child's other parent is not contributing, or pays only sometimes
not_when: a maintenance order already exists and is being paid (then the question is enforcement, same office)
steps: Go to the maintenance office at the magistrate's court nearest to where you live and ask to apply for maintenance
Take your ID, the child's birth certificate, and proof of the child's monthly costs (school, food, clothes, transport, medical) with receipts where you have them
Give the other parent's name, ID number if you know it, address and where they work
Attend the date the court gives; the court can set a monthly amount and order it deducted from their pay
If an order exists and is not paid, go back to the same office with the order number and ask for enforcement
cost: Free at the maintenance office; no lawyer is needed
stakes: Money the child is entitled to, every month, is the cheapest income in the house to claim

title: Asking a creditor for a smaller instalment, in writing
owner_summary: Before you miss a payment, ask the creditor in writing for a smaller instalment for a fixed number of months, say what you can pay, and keep paying that amount from the day you ask. Most lenders have a hardship or arrangements team whose job this is, and a written offer you kept to is the thing that protects you if it ever goes further. Keep every reply. If more than one creditor cannot be paid, the formal route is debt review through a registered debt counsellor, which stops the collectors while it runs; do not pay anyone who promises to make the debt disappear.
applies_when: you can pay something but not the full instalment, on one or two accounts
not_when: you cannot pay anything at all on several accounts (then read the debt review entry)
steps: Work out what you can pay each month on that account without missing food, rent or transport
Write to the creditor (email or their app's message channel): your account number, that you cannot afford the full instalment, the amount you can pay, and for how many months
Pay that amount on the usual date from this month, whether or not they have replied
Keep the letter and every reply in one place on your phone
If they refuse and you have more than one account you cannot pay, ask a registered debt counsellor about debt review before the collectors start
cost: Free to ask; a debt counsellor's fees are set by the NCR (see the debt review entry)
stakes: A missed payment with no arrangement is what starts the collectors and the credit-record listing

title: "You have won": never pay to receive money
owner_summary: Nobody who is really giving you money asks you to pay a fee, airtime or a deposit first, and no real competition you did not enter can pick you as a winner. A message that says you have won and asks for a fee, your ID number, your bank details or an OTP is a scam, however official the logo looks. Do not reply, do not click the link, and never send money to release money. If you already paid, tell your bank straight away and report it at SAPS; if you gave an ID number, ask SAFPS for free protective registration.
applies_when: an SMS, WhatsApp, email or call says you have won something and asks you to do anything first
not_when: a competition you entered yourself, where the organiser asks for nothing before paying out
steps: Do not reply, do not click any link, and do not phone the number in the message
Ask one question: did I enter this? If not, it is a scam
Never pay a fee, buy airtime, or send an ID number, bank details or OTP to receive a prize
If you already paid or sent details, tell your bank's fraud line now and report at SAPS with the message
Block the number and delete the message; if they phone, hang up
cost: Free
stakes: The fee you pay to receive money is money gone, and the details you send are used to open accounts in your name
